articles.description:
WARN Act and Health Insurance: What Happens to Your Coverage After a Layoff


A WARN notice tells you when your job is scheduled to end. It does not, by itself, tell you when your health insurance ends — and that gap catches many workers by surprise. The WARN Act is a notice law, not a benefits law. It requires qualifying employers to give 60 days' advance notice of a mass layoff or plant closing, but it does not set the date your health coverage stops, and it does not pay your premiums.
That makes health coverage a separate question to answer as soon as a notice arrives. The figures below set the scale: as of November 1, 2026, Layoff Atlas tracks 686 WARN notices covering 66,703 reported workers in its 90-day notice window, with 29 counts unavailable. articles.author: Eka Putri
articles.description:
Everyone in my feed read the announcement as a scoreboard: three results, one in maths, one in computer science, one in physics, plus a new arrangement for working with academic labs. I read it twice, then did what I normally do with a release note — I went looking for what is reproducible and what is only claimed.
Two things stood out for me.
First, the interesting part is not the headline result. It is the workflow around it. If a model can propose a candidate, the expensive work moves to verification: who runs the check, on what hardware, and how long until a second team repeats it. I have watched the same shift in code review now that tools generate patches. The bottleneck stops being "can we produce an answer" and becomes "can we trust the answer cheaply enough to ship."
Second, the academic partnership may matter more than the three papers, if it turns out to be real. Shared compute and shared authorship sound generous. They also mean one lab's priorities quietly become the research agenda of everyone who depends on that compute. Worth watching which fields get picked first and which are left waiting.
None of this makes the results fake. It just means the question for people who build things is boring and practical: what evidence would change my mind, and is that evidence reachable by someone outside the lab?
That last part is the one I will keep checking in six months.
articles.title: An AI Lab Published Science Results. Here Is What I Checked First

articles.author: delay.run
articles.description:
If your app exposes an endpoint that another service calls (a webhook, a scheduled job URL, a callback), anyone who discovers the URL can call it too. Signed requests fix that. The sender computes an HMAC of the request with a shared secret, sends it in a header, and you recompute it and compare. Here's how to do it correctly, including the parts most implementations get wrong.
You and the sender share a secret, for example a long random string.
For each request, the sender computes HMAC-SHA256(secret, message), where the message is usually a timestamp plus the raw request body.
The sender puts the signature (and the timestamp) in headers.
You compute the same HMAC over the same message and compare.
If someone changes the body, or doesn't know the secret, the signatures won't match.
The ex…
